title: Champ
subtitle: Irish mashed potato with spring onion
excerpt: The great Irish potato dish: fluffy mashed potato folded through spring onions that have been steeped in hot milk, finished with a generous well of butter in the centre. Simple, satisfying, and far greater than the sum of its parts.

recipe.sourceNotes: Champ is one of the oldest and most beloved dishes of Irish cuisine, predating the potato famine and documented in Irish food writing from the seventeenth century onwards. The name comes from the Old Norse kamp, meaning to press or mash. It is closely related to colcannon, which uses cabbage or kale instead of spring onions. Champ is particularly associated with Northern Ireland and Ulster, where it is traditionally eaten with a well of butter in the centre and eaten from the outside in to preserve the butter.

content.text: The spring onion is added to warm milk rather than raw into the mash. This takes the edge off the raw sharpness and infuses the milk with onion flavour. Use floury potatoes: King Edward or Maris Piper. Drain them very well and dry them in the pan for a minute over low heat before mashing, so the mash is fluffy not watery. Do not be shy with the butter.
Boil the potatoes in well-salted water for 20 to 25 minutes until completely tender. Drain in a colander and return to the dry pan. Shake over low heat for 1 minute to drive off excess steam.
While the potatoes cook, warm the milk in a small saucepan until steaming. Remove from the heat and add the spring onions. Cover and leave to steep for 10 minutes.
Mash the potatoes until smooth. Add the butter in pieces and beat in. Pour over the warm spring onion milk and fold through. Season generously with salt and pepper.
Serve in individual bowls with a well made in the centre. Add a generous knob of butter and let it melt before eating.
